claim: When humans indicate on which hand a tactile stimulus occurred with crossed hands, they often err.
source: When humans indicate on which hand a tactile stimulus occurred, they often err when their hands are crossed.
evidence: This is a well-established finding cited in the abstract and supported by references throughout the manuscript.

claim: The crossed right hand is localized in left space.
source: the crossed right hand is localized in left space
evidence: This is a logical consequence of crossing the right hand to the left side of space, stated as background knowledge.

claim: When participants incorrectly chose the hand stimulated second, they pointed to where that hand had been at the correct, first time point.
source: When participants incorrectly chose the hand stimulated second, they pointed to where that hand had been at the correct, first time point, though no stimulus had occurred at that location.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the study, supported by data analysis in Figures 5-8.

claim: No stimulus had occurred at the location where participants pointed in incorrect trials.
source: though no stimulus had occurred at that location
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental design and the finding that participants pointed to the incorrect hand's position at time 1.

claim: Stimulus localization depended on hand assignment, not vice versa.
source: This behavior suggests that stimulus localization depended on hand assignment, not vice versa.
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The observed behavior is incompatible with the notion of automatic computation of external stimulus location upon occurrence.
source: It is, thus, incompatible with the notion of automatic computation of external stimulus location upon occurrence.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Humans construct external touch location post-hoc and on demand.
source: Instead, humans construct external touch location post-hoc and on demand.
evidence: This is the main theoretical claim of the paper, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The accuracy of pointing or reaching with an arm or finger to a visual target depends on the position of target relative to gaze.
source: For instance, the accuracy of pointing or reaching with an arm or finger to a visual target depends not only on the position of target relative to gaze (Fiehler et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2014), but also on salient world-centered landmarks (Schütz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The accuracy of pointing or reaching with an arm or finger to a visual target depends on salient world-centered landmarks.
source: For instance, the accuracy of pointing or reaching with an arm or finger to a visual target depends not only on the position of target relative to gaze (Fiehler et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2014), but also on salient world-centered landmarks (Schütz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Judgment of visual location during whole-body movement is influenced by a target's position relative to gaze.
source: Similarly, judgment of visual location during whole-body movement is influenced by a target's position relative to gaze, as well as by the location of the target relative to the body (Tramper and Medendorp, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Judgment of visual location during whole-body movement is influenced by the location of the target relative to the body.
source: Similarly, judgment of visual location during whole-body movement is influenced by a target's position relative to gaze, as well as by the location of the target relative to the body (Tramper and Medendorp, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Touch activates specialized sensory receptors embedded in the skin.
source: Touch activates specialized sensory receptors embedded in the skin
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the somatosensory system.

claim: The arrangement of peripheral sensors is reflected in the homuncular organization of primary somatosensory cortex.
source: the arrangement of the peripheral sensors is reflected in the homuncular organization of primary somatosensory cortex (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Roux et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classic and recent research.

claim: The stimulus location in space must be derived by combining skin location and body posture.
source: However, because our body can take various postures, the stimulus location in space – often referred to as its external location – must be derived by combining skin location and body posture, a process termed tactile remapping (Heed et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about tactile processing, supported by citation.

claim: External tactile locations can be coded in a gaze-centered reference frame.
source: Indeed, there is evidence that external tactile locations can be coded in a gaze-centered reference frame (Harrar and Harris, 2010; Mueller and Fiehler, 2014a; Mueller and Fiehler, 2014b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: External tactile locations can be coded relative to anchors such as the head, torso, and hand.
source: but also relative to anchors such as the head, torso, and hand (Alsmith et al., 2017; Heed et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bottom-up features such as the availability of sensory information can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames.
source: Both bottom-up features such as the availability of sensory information (Bernier and Grafton, 2010) and the spatial reliability of a sensory channel (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002), as well as top-down information such as task-constraints (Badde et al., 2016; Schubert et al., 2017), action context (Mueller and Fiehler, 2014b), and cognitive load (Badde et al., 2014) can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The spatial reliability of a sensory channel can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames.
source: Both bottom-up features such as the availability of sensory information (Bernier and Grafton, 2010) and the spatial reliability of a sensory channel (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002), as well as top-down information such as task-constraints (Badde et al., 2016; Schubert et al., 2017), action context (Mueller and Fiehler, 2014b), and cognitive load (Badde et al., 2014) can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Task-constraints can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames.
source: Both bottom-up features such as the availability of sensory information (Bernier and Grafton, 2010) and the spatial reliability of a sensory channel (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002), as well as top-down information such as task-constraints (Badde et al., 2016; Schubert et al., 2017), action context (Mueller and Fiehler, 2014b), and cognitive load (Badde et al., 2014) can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Action context can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames.
source: Both bottom-up features such as the availability of sensory information (Bernier and Grafton, 2010) and the spatial reliability of a sensory channel (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002), as well as top-down information such as task-constraints (Badde et al., 2016; Schubert et al., 2017), action context (Mueller and Fiehler, 2014b), and cognitive load (Badde et al., 2014) can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Cognitive load can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames.
source: Both bottom-up features such as the availability of sensory information (Bernier and Grafton, 2010) and the spatial reliability of a sensory channel (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002), as well as top-down information such as task-constraints (Badde et al., 2016; Schubert et al., 2017), action context (Mueller and Fiehler, 2014b), and cognitive load (Badde et al., 2014) can affect the relative contributions of different reference frames
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: It is currently not known whether all putative codes are always constructed, or whether they are only computed based on demand.
source: Yet, whereas there is widespread consensus that each spatial code can have more or less influence depending on the specific situation, it is currently not known whether all putative codes are always constructed, or whether they are only computed based on demand.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: It has been suggested that the construction of spatial location in touch is an automatic process.
source: For touch, it has been suggested that the construction of spatial location is an automatic process, implying that any tactile input is remapped into an external code, irrespective of its relevance (Heed and Azañón, 2014; Röder et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research proposing this hypothesis.

claim: A task-irrelevant tactile stimulus delivered to a crossed right hand accelerates visual discrimination in the right visual field if it precedes the visual target stimulus by 60 ms.
source: A task-irrelevant tactile stimulus delivered to a crossed right hand accelerates visual discrimination in the right visual field if it precedes the visual target stimulus by 60 ms, but on the left side if it leads by 180 ms or more (Azañón and Soto-Faraco, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A task-irrelevant tactile stimulus delivered to a crossed right hand accelerates visual discrimination on the left side if it leads by 180 ms or more.
source: A task-irrelevant tactile stimulus delivered to a crossed right hand accelerates visual discrimination in the right visual field if it precedes the visual target stimulus by 60 ms, but on the left side if it leads by 180 ms or more (Azañón and Soto-Faraco, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Stimulus confusion is much more prominent when the arms are in a crossed than uncrossed posture in the tactile temporal order judgment task.
source: Notably, stimulus confusion is much more prominent when the arms are in a crossed than uncrossed posture.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the TOJ literature, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Limb crossing affects TOJ, implying that posture cannot be strategically ignored but is automatically incorporated into hand assignment.
source: That limb crossing, nevertheless, affects TOJ implies that posture cannot be strategically ignored, but is automatically incorporated into the hand assignment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the crossing effect in TOJ tasks.

claim: Increasing the distance between the uncrossed hands can slightly reduce errors in TOJ.
source: Increasing the distance between the uncrossed hands can slightly reduce errors in TOJ (Gallace and Spence, 2005; Roberts et al., 2003; Shore et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The TOJ crossing effect is smaller when the hands' positions additionally differ in height or depth.
source: and the TOJ crossing effect is smaller when the hands' positions additionally differ in height or depth (Azañón et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: If a tactile stimulus is presented during an arm movement, and participants indicate the stimulus's location by pointing to its external location after the movement, they make systematic localization errors.
source: For instance, if a tactile stimulus is presented during an arm movement, and participants indicate the stimulus's location by pointing to its external location after the movement, they make systematic localization errors (Dassonville, 1995; Maij et al., 2011b; Maij et al., 2013; Maij et al., 2017; Watanabe et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Localization errors differ for fast and slow movements.
source: Importantly, because these errors differ for fast and slow movements, it has been suggested that participants do not compute the precise spatial location of a stimulus when it occurs, but instead infer spatial location post-hoc by estimating hand location at the perceived time of the tactile stimulus (Maij et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Participants do not compute the precise spatial location of a stimulus when it occurs, but instead infer spatial location post-hoc by estimating hand location at the perceived time of the tactile stimulus.
source: Importantly, because these errors differ for fast and slow movements, it has been suggested that participants do not compute the precise spatial location of a stimulus when it occurs, but instead infer spatial location post-hoc by estimating hand location at the perceived time of the tactile stimulus (Maij et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from previous research, cited here.

claim: TOJ performance declined in the crossed compared to the uncrossed posture.
source: In accordance with previous findings, TOJ performance declined in the crossed compared to the uncrossed posture (Heed and Azañón, 2014)
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Experiment 1, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: TOJ performance depended on the posture at the time of stimulation.
source: and depended on the posture at the time of stimulation (Heed et al., 2015b; Hermosillo et al., 2011)
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Experiment 1, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: A generalized linear mixed model with factors start posture, end posture, and movement phase revealed significance for all main effects and interactions.
source: A generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with factors start posture, end posture, and movement phase revealed significance for all main effects and interactions (see in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: Participants made, on average, more than 15% TOJ errors even with uncrossed hands.
source: Participants made, on average, more than 15% TOJ errors even with uncrossed hands.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Localization is systematically biased in the direction of the movement during the initial part of a movement, and in the opposite direction during the final part of the movement.
source: More specifically, localization is systematically biased in the direction of the movement during the initial part of a movement, and in the opposite direction during the final part of the movement (Dassonville, 1995; Maij et al., 2013; Maij et al., 2017; Watanabe et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and is also observed in the current data.

claim: Bias was comparable across all four posture conditions.
source: Critically, bias was comparable across all four posture conditions (see Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Experiment 1, supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Participants virtually always indicated correctly which hand had received the stimulus in the 1-stimulus control task (average percentage correct, 99.5%).
source: Participants virtually always indicated correctly which hand had received the stimulus (average percentage correct, 99.5%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the 1-stimulus control task.

claim: Localization error curves were indistinguishable between the 1-stimulus and 2-stimulus tasks.
source: Critically, localization error curves were indistinguishable from the task with two stimuli (see Figure 3D), indicating that tactile localization was affected neither by task difficulty nor by other aspects particular to the TOJ task.
evidence: This is an experimental finding comparing the two tasks, supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: Participants consistently pointed to locations scattered around the movement trajectory of the assigned, incorrect hand.
source: Contrary to this prediction, participants consistently pointed to locations scattered around the movement trajectory of the assigned, incorrect hand, indicating that the chosen stimulus had been perceived on the incorrect hand (see Figure 4 for the localization responses of the same participant as shown in Figure 3).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Experiment 1, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Localization errors of incorrect TOJ trials overlapped with localization errors of correct TOJ trials at time 1 for each of the four start and end posture combinations.
source: Localization errors of incorrect TOJ trials overlapped with localization errors of correct TOJ trials at time 1 for each of the four start and end posture combinations.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Experiment 1, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The time shift between localization errors for correct TOJ trials at time 1 and incorrect TOJ trials, averaged across the four posture conditions, was 6 (s.e. 3) ms.
source: The time shift between localization errors for correct TOJ trials at time 1 and incorrect TOJ trials, averaged across the four posture conditions, was 6 (s.e. 3) ms
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The comparison of a model with and without intercept did not provide statistical evidence to reject a zero time shift for time 1.
source: The comparison of a model with and without intercept did not provide statistical evidence to reject a zero time shift (χ2(1)=0.84, p=0.36).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The average time shift between localization errors for correct TOJ trials at time 2 and incorrect TOJ trials was −105 (s.e. 7) ms.
source: In contrast to the results for time 1, the average time shift between localization errors for correct TOJ trials at time 2 and incorrect TOJ trials was −105 (s.e. 7) ms
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: A model without intercept fit the time 2 condition significantly worse than a model with the intercept.
source: and a model without intercept fit this condition significantly worse than a model with the intercept (χ2(1)=19.38, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: The time shift of −105 ms for time 2 closely matches the stimulus SOA of 110 ms.
source: Furthermore, the time shift of −105 ms for time 2 closely matches the stimulus SOA of 110 ms
evidence: This is an observation comparing the measured time shift to the experimental SOA.

claim: Localization errors of the incorrect TOJ trials largely overlapped with the localization errors of correct TOJ trials at time 1 for each of the four SOAs in Experiment 2.
source: Complementing the findings from Experiment 1 and further corroborating the time reconstruction hypothesis, localization errors of the incorrect TOJ trials largely overlapped with the localization errors of correct TOJ trials at time 1 for each of the four SOAs (see Figure 7)
evidence: This is an experimental finding from Experiment 2, supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: A linear mixed model with factors SOA and Reference Time Point revealed a significant main effect of Reference Time Point in Experiment 2.
source: A linear mixed model with factors SOA and Reference Time Point (localization errors for correct TOJ trials computed relative to time 1 vs. time 2) and time shift of the error curve between correct and incorrect TOJ trials as dependent variable revealed a significant main effect of Reference Time Point (χ2(9,10)=21.33, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: A linear mixed model with factors SOA and Reference Time Point revealed a significant Reference Time Point × SOA interaction in Experiment 2.
source: and a significant Reference Time Point × SOA interaction (χ2(7,10)=9.90, p=0.02).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The time shift between localization errors for correct TOJ trials at time 1 and incorrect TOJ trials, averaged across all four SOA conditions in Experiment 2, was 8 ms.
source: The time shift between localization errors for correct TOJ trials at time 1 and incorrect TOJ trials, averaged across all four SOA conditions, was 8 ms.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: An LMM with one common intercept for all SOAs did not fit the data better than a model without an intercept for time 1 in Experiment 2.
source: As in Experiment 1, an LMM with one common intercept for all SOAs did not fit the data better than a model without an intercept (χ2(1)=1.24, p=0.27).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: The average time shifts between localization errors for correct TOJ trials at time 2 and incorrect TOJ trials were −52 (s.e. 12) ms, −75 (s.e. 12) ms, −87 (s.e. 14) ms, and −104 (s.e. 13) ms for the SOA 60, 85, 110, and 135 ms, respectively, in Experiment 2.
source: In contrast, the average time shifts between localization errors for correct TOJ trials at time 2 and incorrect TOJ trials were −52 (s.e. 12) ms, −75 (s.e. 12) ms, −87 (s.e. 14) ms, and −104 (s.e. 13) ms for the SOA 60, 85, 110, and 135 ms, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: A model with a common intercept for all SOAs explained the data significantly better than a model without an intercept for time 2 in Experiment 2.
source: A model with a common intercept for all SOAs explained the data significantly better than a model without an intercept (χ2(1)=29.27, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: A model allowing for different intercepts for each SOA further improved the goodness of fit for time 2 in Experiment 2.
source: A model allowing for different intercepts for each SOA further improved the goodness of fit (χ2(3)=14.3, p=0.003)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of Experiment 2.

claim: Localization error patterns were similar across uncrossed and crossed start and end hand posture conditions.
source: In contrast, localization error patterns were similar across uncrossed and crossed start and end hand posture conditions, suggesting that arm posture during stimulation did not affect localization responses (see Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Arm posture during stimulation did not affect localization responses.
source: In contrast, localization error patterns were similar across uncrossed and crossed start and end hand posture conditions, suggesting that arm posture during stimulation did not affect localization responses (see Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity of localization patterns across postures.

claim: The dissociation between TOJ hand assignment and localization responses indicates that the two phenomena do not reflect the same process.
source: The dissociation between TOJ hand assignment and localization responses indicates that the two phenomena do not reflect the same process.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Not stimulus location determines hand assignment, but vice versa, hand assignment determines perceived stimulus location.
source: Our present finding that participants incorrectly localize tactile stimuli associated with incorrect limb choice, in contrast, implies that not stimulus location determines hand assignment, but vice versa, hand assignment determines perceived stimulus location.
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion of the study, based on the experimental data.

claim: In a study by Badde et al., 2019, participants performed TOJ of tactile stimuli presented to uncrossed and crossed hands and feet.
source: In that study, participants performed TOJ of tactile stimuli presented to uncrossed and crossed hands and feet (Badde et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of a cited study.

claim: In the Badde et al., 2019 study, TOJ errors systematically depended on different anatomical features such as the type (hand or foot) of the correct limb and its body side.
source: These TOJ errors systematically depended on different anatomical features such as the type (hand or foot) of the correct limb and its body side.
evidence: This describes findings from a cited study.

claim: In the Badde et al., 2019 study, neither the side of space of the limb that had received the correct stimulus, nor the spatial distance between stimulus and response limb affected TOJ errors.
source: Critically, neither the side of space of the limb that had received the correct stimulus, nor the spatial distance between stimulus and response limb affected TOJ errors in this task.
evidence: This describes findings from a cited study.

claim: When a brief flash is shown during a smooth pursuit or saccadic eye movement, its localization is perceived with a bias in the direction of the eye movement shortly before and during the first half of the eye movement, and in the opposite direction at the end of the eye movement.
source: When a brief flash is shown during a smooth pursuit or saccadic eye movement, its localization is perceived with a bias in the direction of the eye movement shortly before and during the first half of the eye movement, and in the opposite direction at the end of the eye movement (Matin and Pearce, 1965; reviewed by Schlag and Schlag-Rey, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in vision.

claim: Irrelevant auditory temporal information can influence the perceived location of a flash near the time of saccades and result in a temporal shift of the visual localization error curve.
source: For instance, irrelevant auditory temporal information can influence the perceived location of a flash near the time of saccades and result in a temporal shift of the visual localization error curve (Binda et al., 2010; Maij et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A computational model for temporal-spatial phenomena faithfully replicates the observed spatial biases for both vision and touch.
source: A computational model for these temporal-spatial phenomena faithfully replicates the observed spatial biases for both vision and touch.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: The model assumes temporal uncertainty about tactile stimulus occurrence relative to the arm movement and combines a probability distribution of the possible stimulus time with the perceived arm movement trajectory.
source: Illustrated for the case of tactile localization on the arm, the model assumes temporal uncertainty about tactile stimulus occurrence relative to the arm movement and combines a probability distribution of the possible stimulus time with the perceived arm movement trajectory (Maij et al., 2013; Maij et al., 2017; see Maij et al., 2011b, for the visual analogue).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of a computational model from cited research.

claim: The present results are compatible with the temporal uncertainty model.
source: The present results, too, are compatible with the temporal uncertainty model.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim relating the current findings to a previous model.

claim: Independent of which hand the stimulus was assigned to, the temporal estimate of the tactile stimulus was identical.
source: Independent of which hand the stimulus was assigned to, the temporal estimate of the tactile stimulus was identical, resulting in identical localization error profiles, based on the trajectory of the chosen hand, in correct and incorrect TOJ trials.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Participants chose one hand presumably based on categorical stimulus characteristics such as the stimulated body side.
source: Instead, participants chose one hand presumably based on categorical stimulus characteristics such as the stimulated body side (Badde et al., 2019)
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on inference from the current data and cited research.

claim: Participants combined the time point associated with the first stimulus with the chosen arm's trajectory.
source: and then combined the time point associated with the first stimulus with the chosen arm's trajectory.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: After hand assignment errors, participants effectively referenced a post-hoc constructed spatial location at which no stimulus had ever occurred.
source: After hand assignment errors, participants, thus, effectively referenced a post-hoc constructed spatial location at which no stimulus had ever occurred.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the experimental data.
